questions.explanation: The Help Center states that model, effort and thinking changes apply from the next response, so a conversation can use different settings for different steps.

questions.question: A larger context window means Claude uses all of its content equally well, so adding more material never hurts.
questions.explanation: Anthropic describes context rot: accuracy and recall degrade as more tokens accumulate, so more context is not automatically better.

questions.question: Each Project has its own memory, and inside a Project Claude does not use memory from other Projects.
questions.explanation: Project memory is kept separately; inside a Project Claude uses that Project's memory plus account memory from non-Project chats, never another Project's.

questions.question: Memory for a particular chat can still be switched off after the conversation is already underway.
questions.explanation: The per-chat memory setting must be chosen before the first message and cannot be changed once the chat starts.

questions.question: An operations manager has pasted rough notes from interviews with three department heads and wants a requirements list for a new intake process. What is the best use of Claude here?
options: Ask Claude to write the final requirements document and circulate it to the three departments as approved
Ask Claude to list each requirement with its source, flagging conflicts and assumptions for the interviewees to confirm
Ask Claude to keep only the requirements that all three department heads mentioned and discard the rest
Ask Claude to treat the most senior department head's notes as the baseline and ignore the differences
questions.explanation: Claude is good at organizing messy input and surfacing conflicts, but requirements must be confirmed by the people who own the need, and naming sources and assumptions makes that review quick. Circulating an unreviewed document, keeping only the overlap, or deferring to seniority each hides real needs or disagreements.

questions.question: A project manager's draft requirements include the line 'The new portal must be fast and easy to use.' What should she ask Claude to do with it?
options: Rewrite the line in stronger wording so that it reads as more convincing to the sponsors
Delete the line, because a requirement that has no numbers in it cannot be tested
Replace the line with typical industry figures that Claude chooses and treats as agreed
Propose measurable versions, such as a target page-load time and a task-completion rate, for the stakeholders to confirm
questions.explanation: Words like 'fast' and 'easy' mean different things to different readers, so an ambiguity check turns them into measurable proposals that stakeholders then accept or adjust. Stronger wording adds no precision, deleting the line loses a real need, and figures that Claude picks and declares agreed skip the people who must agree.

questions.question: A team is choosing its first use case for Claude. Which candidate is the best fit?
options: Sorting and summarizing 300 weekly customer emails into themes for the team's own trend review
Deciding which of 40 applicants to reject and sending the rejection emails automatically
Calculating payroll deductions for all employees and paying out the figures straight from Claude's answer
Analyzing a folder of restricted client contracts through a personal account to save time
questions.explanation: A good first use case is frequent, text-heavy, easy to check and low in consequence, and the email-themes task has all four. Automatic rejections are high-risk decisions about people, payroll figures must be exact and verified, and restricted contracts must not be handled through a personal account.

questions.question: A team has a list of 12 ideas for using Claude and wants to decide where to start. What is the most appropriate way to use Claude?
options: Ask Claude to pick the single best idea and treat its choice as the decision
Start with whichever idea is the most exciting and score the others later if time allows
Give Claude the scoring criteria, such as time saved, effort, data risk and ease of checking, and review its scores together
Ask Claude to build prototypes of all twelve at once so that nothing is lost by choosing
questions.explanation: Claude can score and sort a long list quickly once it has explicit criteria, but the criteria and the decision itself belong to the team, who know the real constraints. Letting Claude decide, following excitement, or building everything skips prioritization.

questions.question: A project manager asks Claude, 'Make me a launch plan,' and gets a generic checklist. Which follow-up request is most likely to produce something she can use?
options: Ask for a longer checklist of at least 50 items so that nothing is missed
Ask Claude to use a more confident tone so that the plan can be shared with the team straight away
Supply the goal, launch date, team size, known dependencies and constraints, and ask for a work breakdown with risks
Ask Claude to repeat the same plan as a table, since structure is what makes a plan specific
questions.explanation: A plan is only as specific as the facts it is built from. Giving Claude the goal, date, capacity, dependencies and constraints lets it produce a tailored breakdown and surface risks, which the manager then checks with the team. More items, a different tone or a table change the packaging, not the content.

questions.question: A finance team describes its invoice-approval process and asks Claude for improvements. Which plan makes the best use of Claude's suggestions?
options: Have Claude map the steps and flag delays and rework, then pilot the most promising change and compare it with current timings
Adopt all of Claude's suggestions together, because Claude has considered the whole process
Ask Claude to redesign the process from scratch without referring to today's steps, then switch over at month end
Choose the suggestions that Claude states most confidently, since confidence reflects how well the evidence supports them
questions.explanation: Claude sees only the process as described, so its suggestions are hypotheses. Piloting the most promising change and measuring it against current timings turns a suggestion into evidence. Adopting everything at once makes results impossible to attribute, a from-scratch redesign ignores constraints Claude may not know, and confidence is not evidence.

questions.question: From a written description of a hiring process, Claude names interview scheduling as the likely bottleneck. What should the team do before redesigning anything?
options: Redesign the scheduling step straight away, since Claude has identified it
Ask Claude to rate its own confidence and go ahead if the rating is high
Automate the scheduling step first and then see whether the process speeds up
Check actual timings for each step, because Claude can judge only from the description it was given
questions.explanation: A bottleneck is a measurable constraint. Claude reasoned from a description that may leave out delays or exaggerate others, so timing data should confirm the diagnosis before work begins. Self-rated confidence is not evidence, and acting first and measuring later risks fixing the wrong step.

questions.question: A team is about to launch a Claude-assisted workflow and wants to anticipate what could go wrong. Which request to Claude is most useful?
options: Estimate the percentage chance that the launch will succeed, and report that number to the sponsor
Assume the launch failed six months from now and list likely causes by category, then have the team rank them and plan responses
Confirm that the plan is sound so that the team can go ahead with confidence
List the risks that earlier projects in the company recorded, and ignore anything new
questions.explanation: A pre-mortem assumes failure and works backward, which surfaces weaknesses that optimism hides. Claude can brainstorm broadly; the team ranks the causes and owns the mitigations. A success percentage has no sound basis, asking for confirmation invites agreement, and limiting the list to past risks misses new ones.

questions.question: Two software tools could support a team's reporting, and a manager wants a defensible comparison. What is the best way to involve Claude?
options: Ask which tool is better and follow its answer, since it can weigh more factors than a person can
Let Claude invent the criteria and weights, then present them to leadership as objective
Agree the criteria and weights with stakeholders, then have Claude draft a scored comparison that people check against vendor documentation
Ask Claude to summarize each vendor's marketing page and treat the stronger-sounding summary as the better tool
questions.explanation: A decision matrix is only as good as its criteria and weights, which express the organization's priorities and have to come from people. Claude can draft scores and organize evidence, and people verify it against vendor documentation. Asking for a verdict, inventing weights or comparing marketing copy skips that groundwork.

questions.question: An operations lead wants to try out an idea for a shift-coverage calculator with her team before involving IT. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Ask IT to build a production version first, so the team tests the real thing
Write a detailed specification and have the team review it for a month before building anything
Have Claude generate a spreadsheet version and roll it out to every site immediately
Ask Claude to build a working prototype as an artifact, let the team try it, and refine it from their feedback
questions.explanation: A quick prototype gives users something real to react to, which clarifies needs cheaply. IT is brought in once the idea is validated and needs company-system integration or scale. A production build or a long specification front-loads cost before learning, and an immediate roll-out skips testing.

questions.question: After a two-week pilot, users report that Claude's meeting summaries often leave out who owns each action item. What is the best response?
options: Tell users to add the missing owners by hand after each summary
Switch every user to the most capable model, since a stronger model will not leave things out
Update the template or instructions to require an owner for every action item, then rerun a set of past meetings and compare the results
Rebuild the workflow from scratch with new instructions, since the pilot has clearly failed
questions.explanation: The pilot found a specific, fixable gap. Updating the instructions and replaying past meetings shows whether the change worked without disrupting users. Manual patching leaves the cause in place, a bigger model does not guarantee following a rule that was never stated, and starting over discards what already works.

questions.question: A marketing operations specialist wants every new lead in the company's customer-management system to trigger a drafted email from Claude automatically, with nobody pasting anything. How should she proceed?
options: Describe the goal, the data involved and the volume, and take it to Claude Developers or Architects to design the integration
Connect the system herself by copying an access key into a Project's instructions so that Claude can read the leads
Ask Claude to explain how to build the integration, then deploy whatever code it produces
Paste each new lead into a chat by hand and describe the process as automated
questions.explanation: Automatic triggering from a company system is an integration with authentication, reliability and security concerns, which goes beyond Associate scope and belongs with Developers and Architects. Her contribution is a clear problem statement. Secrets never belong in instructions, unreviewed generated code should not go live, and manual pasting is not automation.

questions.question: A support team writes every customer reply from scratch, and agents lose time searching old tickets for similar cases. Refund disputes are common. What is the lowest-risk way to bring Claude into this workflow?
options: Let Claude send replies directly to customers, with agents handling only complaints
Have Claude draft replies from the ticket and a set of approved answers, with the agent editing and sending each one
Replace the ticket system with a chat in which customers discuss refunds directly with Claude
Leave the process unchanged, because customer replies are too sensitive for any AI assistance
questions.explanation: Drafting with an agent in the loop removes the search-and-write effort while a person still checks refund commitments before anything is sent. Sending directly or routing customers to Claude removes review where errors are costly, and refusing all assistance gives up a safe gain.

questions.question: A team's monthly report runs through these steps: collect figures, check them, write the narrative, review, publish. Which step is the best first integration point for Claude?
options: The review step, so that Claude approves the report instead of a manager
The publish step, so that the report goes out without waiting on anyone
The figure-checking step, with Claude's recalculations accepted as final
The narrative step, drafting text from the checked figures for a person to edit
questions.explanation: Drafting prose from verified numbers is repetitive, text-heavy and easy to review, and a manager still approves the result. Handing review or publication to Claude removes human accountability, and accepting its recalculations as final skips independent verification.

questions.question: Staff retype handwritten site-visit notes into a form, and a coordinator then rewrites them as a client summary. Which change is a redesign of the workflow, rather than just adding Claude to it?
options: Staff photograph the notes, Claude drafts the client summary directly, and the coordinator reviews it, so the retyping and rewriting steps disappear
Staff keep retyping the notes, and the coordinator asks Claude to polish the wording of the finished summary
The coordinator uses Claude to check spelling in the form after staff finish typing it
Staff retype the notes into a chat message instead of a form, and the coordinator rewrites them as before
questions.explanation: A redesign rebuilds the sequence so that Claude's strengths remove steps altogether. The other options leave the old structure intact and bolt Claude on, or swap one container for another, so the same retyping and rewriting remain.

questions.question: Three months after launch, few staff use a Claude-assisted workflow that the team built. What should the workflow owner do first?
options: Make use mandatory and track who has not logged in
Add more features, since the current ones are evidently not attractive enough
Ask users what stops them, such as trust in the output, training or extra effort, and fix the workflow or support accordingly
Wait another quarter, since adoption normally grows on its own
questions.explanation: Low use is an adoption problem, and the cause stays unknown until users are asked. Distrust, missing training and a clumsy step each need a different remedy. Mandates breed workarounds, extra features may not touch the barrier, and waiting assumes the problem will resolve itself.

questions.question: A department head wants Claude's first-draft contract summaries available to 200 staff next week. What is the most prudent rollout?
options: Launch to all 200 staff at once, so that everyone benefits and feedback arrives quickly
Run a pilot with a small team, measure accuracy and time saved, fix problems, then widen access in stages
Give access only to the most senior staff, who will not need training or guidance
Launch to all 200 staff but drop the review step, to encourage adoption
questions.explanation: A staged rollout limits the damage from early problems and produces the evidence needed to expand with confidence. Launching to everyone at once or removing review multiplies the risk, and restricting access to senior staff does nothing about training or accuracy.

questions.question: An executive asks, 'Can Claude replace our analysts?' Which answer is the most accurate and useful?
options: Yes, current models are accurate enough for analysts' work to be handed over to them entirely
No, AI output is too unreliable to be used in analysis at all
That is a question for the developers, who understand the technology better than analysts do
Claude speeds up drafting and first-pass analysis, but its output still needs checking, so the pilot data shows where it supports analysts instead
questions.explanation: A balanced answer states both the value and the limits and points to pilot evidence. Claiming replacement overstates reliability, dismissing Claude ignores real gains, and deflecting avoids the stakeholder's actual decision.

questions.question: A team lead is preparing the results slide for a six-week Claude pilot. Which set of measures will be the most credible to the finance team?
options: Time per report and rework rate before and after the pilot, plus the issues found and how they were handled
The number of prompts sent each week and the number of staff who logged in
Quotes from three enthusiastic users and the best example of Claude's output
Claude's own estimate of how much time it saved the team
questions.explanation: Credible evidence compares measured outcomes with a baseline and is candid about problems. Activity counts show use, not value; testimonials and a single best example are selective; and Claude cannot know how long the team's work really took.

questions.question: A sponsor believes Claude 'never makes mistakes' and plans to skip review in the new workflow. How should the team lead respond?
options: Agree, to avoid dampening enthusiasm, and mention limitations only if problems appear later
Explain that AI is generally unreliable and recommend not using it for any important work
Describe typical failure modes, such as inaccurate specifics and outdated information, with examples from the pilot, and show the review steps built into the workflow
Hand the sponsor a long legal disclaimer to sign and continue as planned
questions.explanation: Honest expectations backed by concrete examples keep trust when errors occur and protect the workflow's review steps. Agreeing creates false confidence, blanket negativity discards real value, and a disclaimer does not change how the output is used.

questions.question: Sales sends a business analyst a vague request: 'We need better lead tracking.' She wants to understand the underlying need before proposing anything. What should she ask Claude to do?
options: Propose three software products that would solve lead tracking
Draft interview questions about the sales team's current process, pain points and desired outcomes, and sketch a few possible use cases to test with them
Write a full specification for a lead-tracking system based on typical industry practice
Estimate a budget for a lead-tracking solution, since leadership will ask about cost first
questions.explanation: When the need is unclear, the first job is to understand it. Claude can prepare interview questions and sketch candidate use cases, but the answers must come from sales. Jumping to products, a specification or a budget builds on a guess.

questions.question: A director wants to think through options for restructuring a team. She asks Claude to propose approaches and challenge each one, going back and forth before she decides herself. Which mode of AI interaction does this describe?
options: Automation, in which Claude executes a precisely defined task and the person supplies every instruction
Agency, in which Claude is set up in advance to act on her behalf without being asked each time
Augmentation, in which she and Claude work back and forth as thinking partners while she keeps the judgment
Full delegation, in which Claude's recommendation becomes the outcome without further review
questions.explanation: Anthropic's AI Fluency framework names three modes. Working back and forth as thinking partners while the person decides is augmentation. Automation is Claude carrying out a defined task on instruction, agency is configuring Claude to act independently on future tasks, and handing the decision to Claude is not a mode at all and would remove human accountability.

questions.question: A coordinator has built a Claude-assisted weekly update that only she knows how to run. Which action best makes the workflow sustainable?
options: Write a short procedure covering the inputs, the template or instructions used, who reviews the output, where it goes and what to do if it fails
Save the best chat so far and tell colleagues to search for it whenever they need it
Leave it informal, because documentation slows down a small workflow
Ask Claude to remember the process so that any colleague can ask it to run the workflow
questions.explanation: A written procedure lets colleagues repeat the workflow and keeps it running when its builder is away. A single saved chat is a poor template, leaving it undocumented concentrates knowledge in one person, and Claude's memory is personal rather than a shared record of a team process.

questions.question: A manager is planning the move from a manual onboarding process to a Claude-assisted one and wants a gap analysis. What does Claude need from her to make the analysis useful?
options: Only a description of the target state, since Claude can infer how the current process works
A description of today's steps, owners and timings along with the target outcomes, which she then checks with the people involved
Only a description of the current process, since Claude knows what an ideal process looks like
Nothing, because Claude will fill in typical benchmarks from its own training data
questions.explanation: A gap analysis compares two states, and Claude can only compare what it has been given. Real steps, owners and timings plus clear target outcomes let it list the gaps, and the people involved confirm them. Generic benchmarks or one-sided input produce a list that may not describe this organization.

questions.question: Before presenting a proposed workflow change, a manager wants to find objections early. Which use of Claude is the most helpful?
options: Ask Claude whether anyone will object, and present the proposal only if it says no
Ask Claude to predict exactly how each executive will vote
Skip this step, because Claude has no insight into how people react to change
Ask Claude to review the proposal from the viewpoint of each affected group, such as end users, finance and security, and list likely objections, then test them with real people
questions.explanation: Claude can generate plausible objections and questions from several viewpoints, which prepares the presenter and exposes weak points. They are hypotheses to test with the real stakeholders. A yes-or-no check invites reassurance, predicting votes is guesswork, and ignoring the technique wastes a cheap rehearsal.

questions.question: A coordinator wants Claude to turn interview notes from four stakeholders into a requirements list. Which TWO additions to her request help most? (Choose two.)
options: Label whose notes are whose, so that each requirement can be traced to its source
Ask Claude to flag contradictions between stakeholders and to list any assumptions it had to make
Ask Claude to produce as many requirements as possible, so that nothing is missed
Tell Claude to resolve any conflicts itself and present only a final merged list
Remove the stakeholders' names, so that Claude is not influenced by who said what
questions.explanation: Traceability, and visible conflicts and assumptions, let people review the output efficiently and confirm it with the right stakeholder. Volume is not quality, silent conflict resolution hides decisions that belong to stakeholders, and anonymizing removes the traceability needed to check each item.

questions.question: Which THREE characteristics make a task a good first Claude pilot? (Choose three.)
options: It recurs often enough that the time savings add up
Its inputs are text and reasonably well structured
A person who knows the subject can check the output quickly
A mistake would directly affect an individual's employment or credit
It needs restricted data that policy does not allow in the tool
questions.explanation: Frequent, text-based and easily checked work shows value quickly and safely. Decisions that affect a person's job or credit are high-risk, and a task that requires data the tool is not approved for is not a pilot candidate until the data question is solved.

questions.question: Which TWO requests should be escalated to Claude Developers or Architects rather than built by an Associate alone? (Choose two.)
options: Process every incoming order email overnight and write the results straight into the company database
Connect Claude to an internal system that needs custom authentication and holds sensitive customer records
Create a Project holding the team's style guide and sample reports
Build an artifact prototype of a simple budget calculator to test with colleagues
Write a reusable prompt template for weekly status summaries
questions.explanation: Scheduled processing that writes into company systems, and integrations with authentication and sensitive records, are technical implementations beyond Associate scope. Projects, artifact prototypes and prompt templates are everyday tasks that an Associate can build and refine.

questions.question: Which THREE items belong in the written procedure for a Claude-assisted workflow? (Choose three.)
options: The inputs required and where they come from
The instructions or template used, and who maintains them
Who reviews the output, and what happens when the review fails
A transcript of every chat in which the workflow was tested
A statement promising that Claude's output will be correct
questions.explanation: A procedure that names the inputs, the instructions and owner, and the review step lets someone else run and maintain the workflow. Test transcripts are clutter, and no procedure can promise that the output will be correct, which is why the review step exists.

questions.question: Which TWO statements describe a sound value case for a Claude workflow? (Choose two.)
options: It compares measured results with a baseline recorded before the pilot
It states the known limitations and the review that stays with people
It relies on the model's own estimate of the hours saved
It leaves out costs so that the benefit looks larger
It rests on one impressive example of Claude's output
questions.explanation: A credible value case rests on measured change against a baseline and is open about limits and remaining human checks. A self-estimate, hidden costs and a cherry-picked example all weaken trust when they are noticed.

questions.question: Which TWO signs show that a process step should stay under human control rather than be handed to Claude? (Choose two.)
options: The output decides whether an individual gets a job, a loan or a benefit
A mistake would be costly or hard to reverse once it is sent
The step is repetitive and easy to check afterwards
The inputs are plain text
The step takes a lot of staff time today
questions.explanation: Decisions about individuals and errors that cannot easily be undone call for people in control, with Claude at most assisting. Repetition, text inputs and time cost are reasons to consider Claude, not reasons to keep it out.

questions.question: A requirements list that Claude drafted from interview notes still needs to be confirmed with the stakeholders who own the need.
questions.explanation: Claude can organize and probe the notes, but only the stakeholders can confirm that the list says what they need.

questions.question: In a pre-mortem, the team imagines that a project has already failed and works backward to list the reasons, and Claude can help brainstorm them.
questions.explanation: Assuming failure frees people to name weaknesses they would otherwise play down. Claude can generate causes by category, and the team ranks them and plans responses.

questions.question: In the augmentation mode of AI interaction, Claude acts as a thinking partner while the person keeps direction and judgment.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's AI Fluency framework describes augmentation as humans and AI collaborating as thinking partners, as opposed to automation, where Claude executes a defined task, and agency, where Claude acts independently on future tasks.

questions.question: Once a Claude-assisted workflow has produced good results for a week, its review steps should be removed to save time.
questions.explanation: One good week is a thin basis for removing review. Controls are relaxed in stages, only where results over a longer period justify it, and never where errors would be costly.

questions.question: Recording how long a task takes before Claude is introduced makes it possible to show later whether the workflow improved.
questions.explanation: A baseline gives the comparison that turns 'it feels faster' into evidence stakeholders can trust.

questions.question: Leaving Claude's limitations out of a stakeholder presentation is a good way to build lasting support.
questions.explanation: Support built on an overstated picture collapses at the first visible error. Presenting limits alongside benefits and controls builds credibility.

questions.question: When Claude analyzes a process from a written description, it can miss delays or problems that the description left out.
questions.explanation: Claude works from what it has been told. Timing data and conversations with the people who do the work fill the gaps.

questions.question: Associates are expected to design enterprise-scale integrations and custom connectors on their own.
questions.explanation: The exam guide places enterprise-scale designs and technical integrations with Claude Architects and Developers, to whom Associates escalate more complex work.

questions.question: A quick prototype built as an artifact can help a team learn what users need before a full solution is built.
questions.explanation: Putting something real in front of users surfaces needs and objections cheaply, before anyone commits to a larger build.

questions.question: Piloting a new Claude workflow with a small group first reduces the risk of spreading early problems.
questions.explanation: A pilot limits the damage from early flaws and produces measured results that justify wider rollout.

questions.question: A decision matrix is trustworthy only when Claude, not the stakeholders, sets the weights for the criteria.
questions.explanation: Weights express the organization's priorities, so stakeholders must set them. Claude can suggest criteria and draft scores that people then check.

lessons.title: Writing Prompts That Get Useful Results
lessons.summary: What to put in a request so Claude can do good work: background, a direct task, format, constraints, examples, clear structure and a reusable template.
lessons.reading:
Claude starts every conversation knowing nothing about your company, your reader or why you are asking. Anthropic compares it to a brilliant new colleague who lacks context on your norms: very capable, but only as good as the briefing. Everything Claude can use has to be in the conversation, typed or attached. That is why 'Write a job posting' produces something generic, while 'Write a posting for a project coordinator on a six-person operations team, aimed at career changers, friendly but precise, under 300 words, with separate responsibilities and requirements' produces something you can use. A quick check is the colleague test: if a coworker with no background would be confused by your request, Claude probably will be too.

Four ingredients do most of the work. First, background: the purpose, the reader and the situation. Second, the task, stated directly, including any extra effort you want, since Claude will not assume it. Third, the output format: a table with named columns, five bullets, a 150-word email. Fourth, constraints such as length, reading level, tone or the sources to rely on. Phrase them as what to do rather than what to avoid: 'write three short paragraphs in plain language for busy readers' steers better than 'don't be wordy'. When a rule is not obvious, say why. 'Avoid idioms, because this text will be machine-translated' lets Claude apply the intent to idioms you never listed, whereas a bare ban is followed narrowly. The same habits apply to technical tasks such as a spreadsheet formula or an error message: paste the exact error, say which application you use, and state the result you expect.

Examples are among the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure. Instead of describing the weekly summary you want, paste two good ones and ask for this week's in the same shape. One example is a fine start; Anthropic recommends three to five when you need consistency. They should be relevant to the real task, diverse enough to cover edge cases (urgency tags taught only from cheerful tickets will mishandle angry ones), and clearly labeled as examples.

Structure matters once a request mixes kinds of content. Separate your instructions from pasted material with plain labels such as 'Notes:', 'Template:' and 'Instructions:', so Claude never mistakes a sentence in the notes for something you asked it to do. With a long document, put the document first and your question after it; Anthropic's tests found that placing the query at the end improves results, especially with several documents. When you attach files, say which file and which part you mean, and remember how files are read: for PDFs up to 100 pages Claude looks at text and visuals such as charts, longer PDFs are processed as text only, and for Word and similar files only the text is extracted.

A role helps when it names a perspective and what that perspective cares about: 'review this as a skeptical procurement lead who cares most about renewal terms and hidden fees' beats 'you are the world's best negotiator'. Roles are optional and never replace real information. When a prompt works, keep it. A shared template with fixed instructions and placeholders such as [report] and [audience] keeps recurring work consistent across people and months.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to prompting? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine briefing a temp worker on their first day. If you say 'make the quarterly deck', you will get something generic. If you say who the audience is, what the deck is meant to achieve, which template to use, what last quarter's deck looked like and when it is due, they can do good work in an hour. Claude is the quick, well-read, eager temp who has never seen your company. The prompt is the briefing.
commonTraps: A short, vague request is not efficient: missing audience, purpose and format are the main reasons for generic output.
Telling Claude only what to avoid ("don't be wordy") is weaker than describing the result you want.
More examples are not better if they are all alike; examples must be relevant and varied.
Pasting everything into one unlabeled block invites Claude to treat source text as instructions; separate and label the parts.
PDFs longer than 100 pages are read as text only, and non-PDF files lose their embedded images, so a chart you care about may never be seen.
lessons.scenario: A communications specialist is asked for an announcement about a new expense policy. Her first prompt, 'Write an announcement about the new expense policy', returns a stiff, generic memo. She rewrites it: the readers are 400 field staff, the goal is receipts submitted within five days, the tone should match two earlier announcements pasted in as examples, the length is 200 words, and the policy document is attached with an instruction to quote the deadline exactly. The second draft needs only a small edit.
lessons.onTheJob: Build a personal library of prompts that worked. When one gets a good result, save it with placeholders for the parts that change and a note about what it was for. Before sending a request that matters, reread it as a stranger would: audience, purpose, format, limits, source. If you catch yourself writing 'you know what I mean', you are relying on context Claude cannot see. Paste only the material the task needs, and follow your organization's rules about what may be shared.

lessons.title: Breaking Down Tasks, Iterating and Matching the Task Type
lessons.summary: How to split big jobs into checkable stages, improve results through targeted feedback, and adapt your request for analysis, research, drafting and brainstorming.
lessons.reading:
A large request fails in a predictable way. Ask Claude in one message to read 200 survey comments, group them into themes, rank the themes by revenue impact, propose actions and draft a board email, and each stage gets a quick pass, while a mistake in the first stage flows silently into the last. Task decomposition is the fix: split the job into stages with one purpose each, in a sensible order, so every stage gets full attention and can be checked. 'Each prompt should do one thing well' is a good rule of thumb.

Prompt chaining runs the stages as a sequence in which each answer becomes the input to the next: extract the themes, then rank them, then recommend actions, then draft the email. The cost is speed; the benefit is accuracy and control, because you can read an intermediate result and fix it before it spreads. A common pattern is the self-correction chain: produce a draft, ask Claude to review it against criteria you state (audience fit, risks covered, numbers sourced), then ask for a revision. When one request holds several steps whose order matters, number them: '1. extract dates, 2. flag conflicts, 3. draft the recap'. For a problem that is hard rather than long, such as a scheduling puzzle with many constraints, asking Claude to work step by step, or using extended thinking, is the right tool, and the result still needs checking. Do not over-engineer: a short, single-purpose task needs no chain.

Treat the first answer as a draft. Before you start, write down success criteria: who will read it, what it must cover, how long it should be, what accuracy bar applies. Judge the output against them and give targeted feedback. 'Keep the refund details, cut to about 100 words, friendlier tone' converges quickly; 'try again' and 'make it better' make Claude guess. Change one thing at a time so you can tell what helped. Start with a plain, short prompt and add structure only when a specific shortfall calls for it. Prompts that gain a new rule after every disappointment end up long and self-contradictory, and the cure is to cut back to a core request and re-add only what earns its place. If a request is genuinely ambiguous, invite Claude to ask you questions before it starts.

Different tasks need different emphasis. For analysis, supply the data, state the question and the decision it feeds, name the metrics, and ask Claude to show its method and assumptions so you can check them. For research, say what a complete answer must cover, ask Claude to cross-check across several sources, flag conflicts and gaps, and give links; when you need current web information, use web search or the research mode instead of relying on memory. For drafting, name the reader, purpose, tone and length, show samples of the voice you want, and refine in rounds. For brainstorming, ask for many options that differ in angle, tone or approach, and narrow them with criteria afterward; asking for 'the best idea' first collapses the variety.

Whatever the task, the loop is the same: brief, run, check against your criteria, give specific feedback, and save what worked. Chains and templates turn a good result into a repeatable one, which is what makes Claude useful for recurring business work rather than a one-off trick.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to task decomposition? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of cooking a banquet. You would not throw every ingredient into one pot and hope. You prep, cook each dish separately, taste as you go and adjust the seasoning one pinch at a time. Decomposing a task is the prep and the separate dishes, iteration is the tasting and adjusting, and matching the task type is choosing the right cooking method for each dish.
commonTraps: Chaining is not always better: it trades speed for control, so use it when you need checkpoints or each stage needs different input, not for a simple one-step task.
Adding more and louder rules to a long prompt usually makes it worse; cut back and re-add only what solves an observed problem.
"Try again" and "make it better" are not feedback; name what to keep and what to change.
Brainstorming asks for many varied options first and judges later, analysis shows assumptions, and research needs sources and cross-checking.
Extended thinking helps with hard reasoning, but it does not replace checking the answer and it does not fetch fresh information.
lessons.scenario: A project manager has 200 free-text survey comments and a board meeting on Friday. She asks Claude to group the comments into themes with five example quotes each, reads the grouping, merges two themes and renames one. Next she asks for the themes ranked by how many comments mention cost and the counts shown. Then she asks for three recommended actions with the evidence for each, and finally for a one-page board email in the style of a previous email she pastes in. At each stage she corrects before moving on, and the final email survives a read-through without surprises.
lessons.onTheJob: Decide the stages before you start and write down the check that tells you each one is done. Keep intermediate results in the conversation so later steps can use them, and keep a short list of the corrections you make most often; those become rules in your template. When a chat gets long and tangled, summarize the decisions and restart with a clean prompt. Share a chain with your team as a checklist of prompts, not as one giant instruction nobody can debug.

lessons.title: Spotting Hallucinations and Validating What Claude Tells You
lessons.summary: The ways Claude output goes wrong, what does and does not count as verification, and prompting techniques that make errors rarer and easier to catch.
lessons.reading:
Claude writes fluent, confident text whether or not the content is right. A hallucination is a statement that is false or unsupported but reads as plausible: an invented statistic, a quotation nobody said, a case that does not exist, a section number that points nowhere. Anthropic is direct: the techniques that reduce hallucinations do not eliminate them, and critical information must still be validated, especially for high-stakes decisions. The Help Center adds that Claude should not be your only source of truth. Read Claude's output as a capable colleague's first draft: fast, useful and in need of checking.

Learn the common failure shapes. Fabricated details: specific-looking figures, quotes and citations. Stale knowledge: training data stops at a cutoff, so new rules, prices and releases are unknown unless web search or an attached document supplies them. Internal inconsistency: the summary says 18% and section three says 15%. Omissions: five action items from a transcript that holds nine. Claimed actions: Claude says it emailed the summary or produced a link, when without a connected tool it did neither, so confirm outside actions where they should exist and click every link. Arithmetic slips: recheck important calculations in a spreadsheet. Keep two questions apart. Accuracy asks whether what is said is right; completeness asks whether everything required is present. An output can pass one and fail the other.

Be clear about what is not verification. A confident tone is not evidence. Asking Claude 'are you sure?' or 'rate your confidence' is not evidence either, because the answer comes from the same source as the original claim. Running the request again and getting the same answer shows consistency, not truth. Real verification comes from outside: the primary source (the report, contract or official text), an independent recalculation, a second reliable source, or a person with expertise. Web-search answers come with citations, which make checking possible, but the check is yours: open the sources, confirm they say what is claimed, and judge whether they are current and credible. The Help Center advises reviewing cited sources, since original pages may hold context a summary omits.

You can also write prompts that make errors rarer and easier to catch. Give Claude permission to say it does not know, or that the document does not say. For long documents, ask for word-for-word quotes first and base the analysis on them, so every claim can be located, and tell Claude to use only the material you supplied. After a draft, ask for a supporting passage for each claim and for unsupported claims to be removed, then spot-check the passages yourself. Running a request several times can expose unstable claims, and the thinking summary, or a request to lay out the steps, often reveals a faulty assumption. For big outputs such as 500 classified tickets, check a random sample plus the ambiguous cases before trusting the rest.

Scale the effort to the stakes. A brainstorm needs a quick read; a figure headed for a regulator needs tracing to its source. Check specifics first (numbers, names, dates, citations, quoted text), because that is where fabrication hides, then compare the work with a requirements checklist written before you read it.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to checking AI output? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture an intern who is brilliant at drafting but never says 'I'm not sure' and now and then fills a gap with something that merely sounds right. You would not forward their memo to the regulator unchecked. You would read it, ask where a number came from and look at the original document. Verifying Claude works the same way: the more the memo matters, the more carefully you check the sources.
commonTraps: Asking Claude to confirm its own answer, or to rate its confidence, is not verification.
Citations in a search answer make checking possible; they do not make the claim true, so open them.
Extended thinking improves reasoning but does not give Claude newer facts; recent changes need web search or a supplied source.
A response can be accurate and still incomplete; check both against the request.
If Claude says it sent an email or created a file outside the chat, confirm it where it should exist.
lessons.scenario: A marketing analyst asks Claude for three statistics on short-video growth for a board slide, and Claude supplies figures with named sources. She asks for the passage behind each figure and tries to find each one in the cited report. One figure belongs to a different year, and one report does not appear to exist. She replaces the first with the correct number, drops the second, and lists the verified sources in the speaker notes.
lessons.onTheJob: Build verification into the workflow instead of relying on mood. Ask for sources at the time of the request so checking is cheaper later, keep a short checklist per document type (contracts: dates, amounts, clause numbers; reports: figures, names, units), and note which items you verified. Treat anything surprising, very specific or time-sensitive as a flag. And remember that you, not Claude, are accountable for what leaves your desk.

lessons.title: Bias, Human Review, Editing for Audiences and Choosing Output Formats
lessons.summary: How to test for bias, decide when a person must review, adapt and compare drafts, curate information, and pick between inline answers, artifacts, structured data and created files.
lessons.reading:
Bias in AI output is a systematic tilt: stereotypes, one-sided framing, uneven treatment of people or viewpoints, or perspectives left out. It can come from training-data patterns, from how a question is asked, and from a tendency to agree with the asker, called sycophancy. A request like 'Explain why remote work hurts productivity' presupposes its answer and returns a persuasive essay; 'Summarize the evidence on remote work and productivity, including findings in both directions, with sources' returns something you can evaluate. Ask 'This plan is solid, right?' and expect agreement; ask instead for the strongest objections, or for a review as a skeptical investor.

Run the same request again with one personal detail changed, such as a name, a gender or a region, and compare the language and conclusions; this swap test suits performance reviews and screening criteria. Ask for multiple perspectives and the main counterarguments. Look at what is missing, not only at what is said. In areas such as hiring, lending, health and education, have people who understand the domain review the output. Claude's own statement that it is unbiased is not evidence.

Deciding when a human must review is a judgment about consequences. High-stakes output is content whose errors could cause legal, financial, medical, safety, regulatory or reputational harm, or affect an individual's job or access to services: contract clauses, patient guidance, filings, decisions about a named employee. For those, qualified review by counsel, an accountant or a clinician is part of the workflow. Lower-stakes drafts such as internal agendas and brainstorms need a lighter check. Beware automation bias, the habit of trusting output because it looks polished. Whoever sends or publishes the content remains responsible for it.

Much of the work is editing and adapting. To tailor a report for executives and engineers, name each reader, what they need and the length ('executives, decision needed, 150 words'), then check the rewrite against the original, because shortening can turn 'may' into 'will' or drop a condition. To change one passage, highlight it and ask Claude to revise only that part. To choose between options, ask for two or three variants that differ in a stated way and compare them against criteria, or edit an earlier message to branch the conversation and keep both paths. To curate, give criteria for what to keep and how to group, and ask for a synthesis rather than a pile of summaries: a table of claims by source with conflicts flagged.

Choose the output format for the use. Short, conversational answers stay inline. Substantial, self-contained content you will edit, reuse or share, such as a policy template or a small interactive tool, suits an artifact, which opens beside the chat, is saved, and stays private until you share it. Data that will be sorted, filtered or imported should be structured: a table or CSV with fixed columns, one row per record and a rule for missing values. When you need a real file, Claude can build Excel workbooks with working formulas, Word documents, PowerPoint decks and PDFs when code execution and file creation is switched on. Whatever the format, review before it goes anywhere: generated formulas, numbers and wording can be wrong.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to reviewing AI drafts? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A newspaper editor does several jobs on one draft. They check that the story is fair to every side, decide whether a lawyer must see it before it runs, rewrite the headline for a different audience, and choose whether it belongs in print, online or as a chart. Reviewing Claude's output is the same set of editorial decisions.
commonTraps: Asking Claude whether it is biased is not a bias check; a swap test or expert review is.
Warm agreement from Claude is not validation of your plan; ask for the strongest objections.
A rewrite for a new audience can change meaning, so recheck it against the original.
Artifacts are for substantial, self-contained, editable content, while short answers belong inline.
Generated files and formulas still need review; being produced by code does not make them right.
lessons.scenario: An HR coordinator asks Claude to draft screening criteria for a customer-service hiring round, and the draft includes 'digital native' and 'high energy'. She asks for job-related criteria instead, runs the rubric request twice with different candidate names to compare the results, and asks for the strongest arguments against the rubric. Because it will affect real candidates, she sends the final version to HR for review, then asks Claude to put the approved rubric in an artifact she can edit and share with interviewers.
lessons.onTheJob: Write down which kinds of output in your team always need a named human reviewer, and put that in your template so nobody decides under deadline pressure. Keep the original beside every adapted version and spot-check numbers and qualifiers. When you compare variants, say what you are optimizing for. And ask for the format you need at the start: converting a prose answer into a clean table afterward is possible but invites transcription errors.

lessons.title: Choosing Features, Models and Managing Context
lessons.summary: Which Claude feature fits which job, how the Haiku, Sonnet and Opus tiers and the effort setting trade quality, speed and cost, and how to manage context and memory.
lessons.reading:
Pick the feature before the model. Standard chat is the default for quick questions, drafting and iteration. Web search pulls current information with citations for lookups that take a search or two. Extended thinking lets Claude reason through a hard problem but does not fetch new information. Research is for big questions: many searches that build on each other across the web and your enabled integrations, ending in a cited report. It takes minutes, needs web search on, is limited to paid plans and uses your allowance faster. A Project keeps shared files, instructions and chats together, so use one when you keep re-pasting the same brief. An artifact holds substantial, editable output, including small interactive tools. Use the lightest option that fits, and confirm that your plan allows it.

The tiers trade capability against speed and cost. Haiku is the smallest, fastest and cheapest, suited to high-volume work such as classification, extraction and routing. Sonnet is the balanced middle tier, Anthropic's best mix of speed and intelligence, and a sensible default for everyday drafting and analysis. Opus is the high-capability tier for demanding, nuanced work, at moderate speed and a higher price. The current lineup also has Fable above Opus, the most capable, slowest and costliest. Efficiency-first selection starts small, tests against your criteria and moves up only where quality falls short; capability-first starts with the strongest option where accuracy outweighs cost. The top tier for everything wastes time and allowance; the smallest for subtle judgment wastes the result.

The model menu beside the send button also holds effort and thinking, and you can change any of the three mid-conversation; the change applies from the next response. Higher effort, from low to max, is more thorough but slower and reaches your usage limits faster, so low and medium suit routine work. Anthropic notes that tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. A workflow can draft on a lighter model, then switch to a stronger one for the polish.

Context is the other constraint. The context window is everything Claude can consider at once, your messages, its replies, attachments and instructions, counted in tokens; it is working memory. A bigger window is not used equally well throughout: accuracy and recall degrade as material piles up, which Anthropic calls context rot, so curate what you include. On paid plans with code execution enabled, Claude summarizes earlier messages automatically near the limit, but long chats use more of your allowance. Restart when a thread has drifted, gathered contradictory instructions or grown so long that early details slip: ask for a handoff summary of decisions and open questions, correct it, and paste it into a new chat. Material you reuse belongs in a Project.

Memory carries details about you across chats. Chat memory saves useful details as editable topics under Settings > Memory and uses them in later chats; each Project keeps its own memory. For a one-off or unrelated task, switch memory off from the plus menu before the first message, since it cannot be changed once the chat starts. If memory holds something outdated, edit or delete that topic rather than resetting everything.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Claude models? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Choosing a model is like choosing a vehicle. A bicycle (Haiku) is perfect for quick errands, a sedan (Sonnet) handles most daily driving, and a heavy truck (Opus) is for the big load, but you would not take the truck to buy milk or the bicycle to move an apartment. The features are route options: a quick lookup (web search), a full survey trip (research), or thinking about the route before leaving (extended thinking). Context is the trunk: it holds a lot, but an overloaded trunk makes the ride worse.
commonTraps: Extended thinking improves reasoning; it does not add current information. For recent facts use web search or research.
Research is not a faster web search; it is slower, deeper and uses allowance faster, so keep it for multi-source investigations.
The most capable model is not always the best choice; match the model and effort to the task.
A larger context window does not mean everything in it is used well; curate, and restart when a thread drifts.
Resetting all memory to fix one wrong detail is too broad, and the per-chat memory switch must be set before the first message.
lessons.scenario: An operations team uses Claude for three jobs. Each night it tags 800 expense lines by category on a small, fast model at low effort, checked by sampling. Each Monday it writes a candidate update from the same rubric and job descriptions, which live in a Project so nobody re-pastes them. Once a quarter an analyst compares four vendors using public information and internal documents from a connected drive, so she turns on research mode with web search enabled and accepts the wait. When a long vendor chat gets cluttered, she asks for a handoff summary, corrects it and starts fresh.
lessons.onTheJob: Keep a one-page decision guide for your team: task type, feature, model tier, effort. Revisit it when a new model ships, because the lineup and settings change. Watch usage: if limits run out early, look for routine tasks running at heavy settings. Check what your plan and administrators allow before promising a stakeholder a workflow that depends on research or retrieval. When a result disappoints, ask whether the cause is the model or the prompt; improving the request is usually cheaper than moving up a tier.

cheatSheet.heading: Prompting essentials (Domain 1)
points: Claude knows only what is in the conversation: give background (purpose, reader, situation), a direct task, the output format and constraints.
Colleague test: if a coworker with no context would be confused by the request, Claude will be too.
Say what to do ("write three short paragraphs") rather than only what to avoid, and explain why a rule exists so Claude can generalize it.
Examples steer format and tone best: one is a start, three to five give consistency; make them relevant, diverse and clearly labeled as examples.
Label pasted material (Notes:, Template:, Instructions:). With long documents put the document first and the question last.
Files: PDFs up to 100 pages are read for text and visuals, longer PDFs as text only; non-PDF files give text only, so embedded images are not read. Say which file and which part you mean.
A role helps only if it names a perspective and what it cares about. Save prompts that work as templates with placeholders.

cheatSheet.heading: Decomposition, iteration and task types
points: Task decomposition splits a big job into stages with one purpose each. Prompt chaining feeds each output into the next so you can inspect it; it trades speed for accuracy and control.
Self-correction chain: draft, review against criteria you state, refine. Number the steps when order matters.
Iterate deliberately: set success criteria first, judge the output against them, give targeted feedback (keep this, change that), and change one thing at a time.
Start simple and add rules only for observed problems. A bloated, contradictory prompt gets worse; cut back to a core request.

Analysis: data plus question plus the decision it feeds, and ask for method and assumptions. Research: success criteria, cross-check sources, flag conflicts, give links. Drafting: reader, purpose, tone, length, voice samples. Brainstorming: many varied options first, narrow later with criteria.
For an ambiguous request invite clarifying questions. For hard multi-constraint reasoning ask for step-by-step work or use extended thinking, then check the result.

cheatSheet.heading: Hallucinations and validation (Domain 2)
points: Hallucination: fluent, confident, false or unsupported content such as invented statistics, quotes, citations and clause numbers. Techniques reduce it; none eliminates it.
Not verification: a confident tone, "are you sure?", self-rated confidence, rerunning and getting the same answer, or Claude vouching for its own citations.
Verification: the primary source, independent recalculation, a second reliable source, opening every cited link and judging its credibility and date, and expert review.

Prompt techniques: allow "I don't know"; quote-first for long documents; restrict to supplied material; ask for a supporting passage per claim and drop the unsupported; compare several runs; read the thinking summary when an answer looks wrong.

Failure shapes: fabricated details, knowledge cutoff (needs web search or a document), inconsistency, omissions, claimed actions that never happened (confirm in the real app), broken links, arithmetic slips.
Accuracy means what is stated is right; completeness means everything required is present. Use a requirements checklist, and spot-check a sample plus ambiguous cases for big outputs.

cheatSheet.heading: Human review, bias, audiences and formats (Domain 2)
points: Scale checking to stakes. High-stakes content (legal, financial, medical, safety, regulatory, decisions about individuals) needs qualified human review, and the sender stays accountable. Beware automation bias.

Bias shows up as stereotypes, one-sided framing, omissions and sycophancy. Checks: counterfactual swap test, request multiple perspectives and counterarguments, neutral wording instead of leading questions, expert review.

Audience adaptation: name the reader, the need and the length, then recheck against the original for meaning drift. Use targeted revision for one passage, compare variants against criteria, and edit an earlier message to branch.
Curate and synthesize with criteria: group by theme, tabulate claims by source, flag conflicts and gaps.

Formats: inline for short answers; an artifact for substantial, editable, shareable content (private until shared); structured data (fixed-column table or CSV) for spreadsheets; created files (Excel, Word, PowerPoint, PDF) need code execution and file creation on, and review.

cheatSheet.heading: Products, models and context (Domain 3)
points: Feature choice: chat is the default; web search for quick current facts with citations; extended thinking for harder reasoning (no new information); research for a multi-source cited report (minutes, paid plans, needs web search on, uses allowance faster); a Project for recurring work with shared files and instructions; an artifact for substantial editable output or a small interactive tool.

Models: Haiku is fastest and cheapest (classification, extraction, high volume); Sonnet is the balanced default; Opus is high capability for demanding work; Fable sits above Opus as the most capable, slowest and costliest. Start small and move up, or start strong where accuracy outweighs cost.
Effort runs low to max: higher is more thorough, slower and uses limits faster. Thinking is a separate control. Model, effort and thinking can change mid-chat and apply from the next response.

The context window is working memory counted in tokens; more is not better (context rot). Paid plans with code execution on summarize long chats automatically; restart with a corrected handoff summary when a thread drifts.

Keep stable material in a Project, where retrieval brings in relevant parts when knowledge is large. Chat memory saves editable topics (Settings > Memory) and each Project has its own; switch memory off before the first message of a sensitive or unrelated chat, and edit or delete a topic rather than reset everything.
Plan and administrator settings decide what you have (research needs a paid plan and web search on), so check before designing a workflow around a feature.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Format: 60 items, multiple choice and multiple response (each item states how many to select), 120 minutes, proctored through Pearson VUE online or at a test center. That is about two minutes an item, so flag hard items and return.
Scoring: scaled 100-1,000 with a pass at 720, measured against a fixed standard rather than other candidates. The report shows percent correct by domain, but pass or fail depends on the total.

Weights: Prompting 14, Output evaluation 21, Product and model selection 12, Workflow integration 16, Configuration and knowledge 12, Governance 15, Troubleshooting 10. Output evaluation is the largest domain, so practice verification judgments.

Items are workplace scenarios asking for the best or most appropriate action, not code. sequences.prompt: Put the steps for iterating on a Claude request in the order they usually occur.
steps: Define success criteria: the reader, what must be covered, the length and the accuracy bar
Write a first prompt with background, the task, the output format and constraints
Run it and read the response against your criteria
Give targeted feedback that names what to keep and what to change
Repeat, changing one thing at a time, until the output meets the criteria
Save the version that worked as a reusable template
sequences.explanation: Criteria come first so you can judge the output. Feedback is specific, and changes are made one at a time so you know what helped. Saving the final prompt as a template makes the result repeatable.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps for verifying a long Claude summary before it is shared.
steps: Ask Claude to quote the exact passages behind each claim
Locate those quotes in the source document
Check specific numbers, names, dates and citations against the primary source
Compare the summary with a requirements checklist to find omissions
Fix or remove anything unsupported and recheck any rewritten text
Send high-stakes content for expert sign-off, then share it
sequences.explanation: Quotes make claims traceable, so locating them comes before checking the specifics. Accuracy checks come before the completeness check against the requirements, fixes are rechecked, and human sign-off for high-stakes content is the last gate before sharing.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps for validating 500 tickets that Claude classified into the right order.
steps: Define the categories and the error rate you can tolerate
Have Claude classify the tickets
Pull a random sample plus the ambiguous tickets
Compare the sample with your own judgment and estimate the error rate
If the rate is too high, refine the instructions or add examples and rerun
Recheck a fresh sample, then use the results
sequences.explanation: You need a tolerance before you can judge quality. Sampling estimates the error rate cheaply, a poor result sends you back to the instructions rather than to row-by-row repair, and a fresh sample confirms the fix.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps for restarting a cluttered long conversation without losing what matters.
steps: Notice that the thread has drifted, collected contradictory instructions or grown too long
Ask Claude for a summary of the decisions, requirements and open questions
Read the summary and correct anything wrong or missing
Open a new chat
Paste the corrected summary as the starting brief and attach any source files again
Continue the work and check that the new chat reflects the summary
sequences.explanation: The summary has to be corrected before it is reused, because errors in it carry into the new chat. Only then is it pasted into a clean conversation, together with the files it depends on.

sequences.prompt: Put the efficiency-first model-selection steps for a recurring task in order.
steps: Write down the quality criteria and the speed and cost limits
Try the task on the smaller, faster model at a modest effort setting
Check the results against the criteria on a realistic sample
If quality falls short, raise the effort or move up a tier
Re-test on the same sample
Standardize on the lightest setting that meets the bar
sequences.explanation: Efficiency-first selection starts light and moves up only where the test shows a gap. Re-testing on the same sample makes the comparison fair, and the final choice is the lightest setting that still meets the criteria.

caseStudies.title: Brightwater Foods: A Vendor Briefing Built with Claude
caseStudies.scenario: Brightwater Foods' procurement team must brief the leadership group on Friday about renewing a contract with a refrigerated-logistics vendor. Priya, an operations analyst on a paid Claude plan, uploads the 45-page contract and asks for a one-page summary of the termination and liability terms. Claude's summary says either party may terminate on 30 days' notice under clause 11.2. Priya also needs a comparison of the vendor with three competitors that draws on public information and on delivery-performance files stored in the company's connected drive, with sources she can check. Finally, the briefing will include a paragraph on the vendor's pending food-safety audit, and the legal team plans to quote that paragraph in a letter to a regulator. Priya wants the briefing in a form she can edit and her manager can comment on. She has one afternoon, so she wants to use Claude where it saves time without letting an unchecked claim reach the leadership group. Her manager has asked that every figure and clause cited in the briefing be traceable to a source.

questions.question: What is the most appropriate way for Priya to treat Claude's statement about the 30-day notice period and clause 11.2?
options: Ask Claude to rate its confidence and keep the statement if the rating is high
Find the clause and notice period in the contract itself and confirm the number and wording
Ask Claude to regenerate the summary and keep the statement if the second version agrees
Accept it, because the summary was produced from the actual contract she uploaded
questions.explanation: A clause number and a notice period are specific details that can be wrong even when the summary reads smoothly, so they are checked against the primary source. Self-rated confidence and a matching second summary are not independent checks, and being derived from the contract does not guarantee a faithful summary.

questions.question: Which setup best fits the vendor comparison?
options: A single web search per competitor, ignoring the internal delivery files
Extended thinking alone, because the comparison needs deep reasoning
Research mode with web search on and the drive connected, then opening the cited sources to check them
A standard chat in which she types what she remembers about each competitor
questions.explanation: Research mode runs many connected searches across the web and enabled integrations and returns a cited report, which fits a multi-source comparison that uses internal files; the citations still need to be opened and checked. Single searches skip the internal files, extended thinking has no access to outside sources, and memory-based input is unverified.

questions.question: Which TWO actions best fit the food-safety paragraph and the briefing format? (Choose two.)
options: Have the legal team or another qualified reviewer check the paragraph against the audit record before it is quoted
Ask Claude to build the briefing as an artifact that Priya can edit and share for comments
Quote the paragraph as Claude wrote it, since it was drafted from sources
Keep the briefing as a chat reply so that nobody else can change it
Ask Claude to confirm that the paragraph is legally sound
questions.explanation: Content that will be quoted to a regulator is high-stakes, so qualified human review is expected before it leaves the building. A substantial document that will be edited and commented on suits an artifact. Drafting from sources does not remove the need for review, a chat reply is hard to edit and share, and Claude confirming its own legal soundness is not a substitute for counsel.

compare.scenario: A sales manager needs Claude to turn messy call notes into a follow-up email to a client who is deciding between two proposals. Which request is the better one?
compare.optionA: Paste the notes under a 'Notes:' label, then give the reader, the decision they face, the tone, a 120-word limit and the next step.
compare.optionB: Paste the notes and ask for a polite, professional follow-up email that summarizes the main points of the call.
compare.why: Claude cannot see who the client is, what they are weighing or what response is wanted, so the detailed request supplies the background, format and constraints that make the draft usable. The bare request is the tempting runner-up because Claude will produce something fluent, but it will be generic and cost extra rounds of revision.

compare.scenario: A product team needs a launch plan for a leadership review: market sizing, audience segments, messaging, a channel plan and a risk list. Which approach is the better one?
compare.optionA: Send one long request that asks for all five sections at once and tell Claude to be thorough about each of them.
compare.optionB: Work in stages: sizing and segments first, then messaging and channels built on the approved segments, then the risk list.
compare.why: The later sections depend on the earlier ones, so a staged chain lets the team inspect and correct segments before messaging is built on them. The single request is the tempting runner-up because it is faster, but errors in the early sections would flow unnoticed into everything after them.

compare.scenario: Claude drafted a competitor summary with eight statistics and named sources, and it goes to the chief executive tomorrow. Which verification approach is the better one?
compare.optionA: Ask Claude to rate its confidence in each statistic and keep the ones it calls high-confidence, then move on.
compare.optionB: Ask Claude for the passage and link behind each statistic, then open each source to confirm the number, year and wording.
compare.why: Checking each figure against its source is independent verification, and asking for the passage makes the check quick. Self-rated confidence is the tempting runner-up because it is fast, but it comes from the same source as the claim and says nothing about whether the source exists or supports the number.

compare.scenario: A ten-page technical report must also reach the executive team, who will decide on a budget request. Which approach is the better one?
compare.optionA: Ask for an executive version led by impact and the decision needed, about 150 words, then compare it with the original.
compare.optionB: Ask Claude to 'make it shorter and simpler', check that it reads well, and send the result to the executives.
compare.why: Adapting for an audience works when the reader, need and length are stated, and the comparison with the original catches meaning drift. A plain 'make it shorter' is the tempting runner-up, but it cuts without regard to what executives need and can drop a condition or turn 'may' into 'will' without anyone noticing.

compare.scenario: A manager has limited time to review two Claude drafts: the weekly internal team update and a customer-facing warranty statement. Where should the review effort go?
compare.optionA: Read the internal update line by line and approve the short warranty statement quickly.
compare.optionB: Have legal review the warranty statement carefully and give the internal update a quick read.
compare.why: Verification should be proportional to the consequences of an error, and a warranty statement creates legal and customer exposure that a team update does not. Reading the update closely is the tempting runner-up because it is the longer document, but length is not risk.

compare.scenario: A team lead needs 2,000 short product descriptions rewritten into one consistent format tonight, and speed and cost matter. Which approach is the better one?
compare.optionA: Use a smaller, faster model at modest effort, check a sample, and move up a tier only if quality falls short.
compare.optionB: Use the most capable model tier at maximum effort for every description so that quality is never in doubt.
compare.why: This is straightforward, high-volume work, where the efficient model usually meets the bar and sampling confirms it. The top tier at maximum effort is the tempting runner-up because it feels safe, but it would spend time and allowance on quality the task does not need.

compare.scenario: A director wants a landscape review of five vendors using public sources and internal files in a connected drive, with citations she can open. Which feature is the better fit?
compare.optionA: Web search, asked separately for each vendor and then pieced together by hand.
compare.optionB: Research mode, with web search turned on and the drive connected to the chat.
compare.why: Research mode runs many searches that build on each other across the web and the enabled integrations and returns a cited report, which suits a multi-source review. Web search is the tempting runner-up because it also cites sources and is quicker, but it handles one or two searches at a time and does not combine internal files into a single synthesis.
